news.2026-11-13-iran-trump-plus-besoin-a: War with Iran: Trump says he no longer “needs” a deal and pulls Vance from the talks, oil rebounds 3%

On Thursday, November 12, Donald Trump says the United States no longer “needs” a deal with Iran and asks Vice President J.D. Vance, who had been leading the talks, to focus on something else. The blockade of Iranian ports continues. Brent, the European oil benchmark, ended the session up 3.3%, at nearly $96 [1][2][4].

On his Truth Social network, Trump wrote: “We have their money, hundreds of billions of dollars, and we have their strait!”, referring to the Strait of Hormuz [1][2]. He also asks Vance to focus on corruption in Democratic cities [3][8].

A change of tone: in recent weeks Trump had been repeating that a deal remained possible after the midterm elections [8]. Yet he admits that leaving with the regime still in place would be “a defeat” [8].

After meeting Qatar’s Prime Minister, Trump wrote that Qatar and other Gulf countries preferred the status quo, meaning the continuation of the US naval blockade [2]. He says he would not hesitate to strike again if “things went the other way” [7].

In the strait, the Iranian army says four tankers were hit by explosions after ignoring its warnings and entering areas it deems off-limits [5]. Two supertankers were reportedly put out of action on Wednesday evening on an “unauthorized route”; nothing has been independently verified [10].

In Tehran, Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf repeats that Hormuz will not return to its former status and that “the ball is now in the American court” [6]. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi insists: “Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same” [8].

According to Israeli media, Benjamin Netanyahu’s security cabinet has ordered the army to prepare for a possible attack [6]. Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warns that any base involved, “from West Asia to Europe,” would be targeted [6].
On Friday, November 13, Brent was trading around $95.41, still on course for a second weekly decline, even as Washington maintains its blockade [9].

Key takeaway: by turning his back on a quick deal, Trump is betting on economically strangling Iran through the blockade rather than on negotiating to reopen Hormuz, which prolongs uncertainty over a key passage for Gulf oil [1][2].

The message remains ambiguous: according to CNN, the two sides were still quietly negotiating, and the White House does not say whether the talks have stopped [3][8]. According to the Wall Street Journal, the administration is divided between resuming talks and keeping the blockade [11].

Secretary of State Marco Rubio considers economic pressure effective enough to avoid major military operations [6]. In Israel, Channel 12 reports a disagreement between Netanyahu and Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir over action against Iran [6].

For you, every message about Hormuz ends up at the pump: a Brent rising back toward $96 slows the decline in gasoline and diesel prices. As long as the strait stays closed, Europe’s energy bill depends on Trump’s next message.

Germany: Mercedes-Benz freezes all new investment in its German plants and weighs closures

On Thursday, November 12, Mercedes-Benz told its employees it was halting all new investment at its German sites, for lack of agreement with employee representatives on cutting labor costs. Management is examining which plants it would have to close if nothing changes [1][2].
“The board of management has jointly decided to stop all new investment in the German sites,” announced Michael Schiebe, a member of the carmaker’s board [2][3].
The trigger: management cannot reach agreement with the works council and the unions on a reduction in labor costs [2].
Mercedes is “carefully examining” which German sites it would have to close if it does not obtain a change in its cost structure. The plants concerned are not known [2].
In September, Michael Schiebe had already warned that two plants in Germany could close without progress in the talks [2].
According to Mercedes, an hour of work in its German plants can cost up to five times more than at its Eastern European sites [2].

Management says it still hopes for a breakthrough: “We want the next generations of vehicles to also be built at our German sites,” says Michael Schiebe [2]. Some media describe the freeze as “temporary” [1][4].
Key takeaway: one of the symbols of German industry openly threatens to close plants in its own country, a sign of the scale of the European auto crisis [1][2].
Like its German competitors, Mercedes is hit by Chinese competition and high costs. Last month, it became the third major German carmaker to lower its outlook for the year [2].
The investment freeze is a pressure tactic in the negotiation: without new investment, a plant does not receive future models, and its future darkens [2][4].
Management’s central argument is the cost gap with its Eastern European plants, up to five times, which makes the historic German sites less competitive [2].

For you, in France, the direct effect is limited, but the German auto industry keeps many European subcontractors busy, including French ones. And it is a signal: if Germany is considering closures, French plants, with similar costs, face the same pressures.

Gaza: an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital kills six people, including a surgeon, and a baby dies of cold in a tent

In the night from Wednesday to Thursday, November 12, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza, killed at least six people, including a surgeon and a teenager. Israel says it targeted a Hamas commander. The same day, a nine-month-old baby died of cold [1][2][3].

Among the dead is surgeon Rezik Abushira; the strike left about 20 injured according to The National, 27 according to the UN, which describes major damage [2][3]. A teenager is also among the victims, according to medical staff [1].

The Israeli army says it targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom it describes as “the commander of Hamas’s Khan Younis brigade,” and accuses the movement of having “turned the Nasser Hospital compound into a headquarters” [3][4]. Hamas rejects the accusation [4]. Nothing so far confirms that this commander was killed [3].
According to Al Jazeera, Nasser is the only hospital still standing in Khan Younis, and the facility has been hit at least seven times since the start of the war [5].

In the same city, a nine-month-old baby, Kinan Ahmed Raqiq, died of hypothermia (a body that has become too cold) in his displaced family’s tent, according to a doctor [8]. The previous weekend, strong storms had caused flooding and the deadly collapse of a sand dune [1].

According to the UN, 94% of Gaza’s residents urgently need shelter, 65% of households live in tents or makeshift shelters, and 650,000 children need help for the winter (warm clothes, blankets) [1]. UNICEF is asking for $97.5 million for its 2026-2027 winter plan [1].

The UN Secretary-General warns that the recent rise in military operations threatens a “fragile” ceasefire [2]. On Thursday, a group of 53 countries and organizations, including Turkey, asked Israel to let humanitarian aid in without restriction [7].
“What kind of ceasefire is this?” reacted the chief executive of the charity Medical Aid for Palestinians, who is calling for British sanctions [6].
Key takeaway: more than a year after the October 2025 ceasefire, strikes continue in Gaza and winter worsens a humanitarian crisis in which most residents still live in tents [1][3].

According to Gaza’s health authorities, at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli attacks since the ceasefire began [3]. Israel replies that it targets fighters hiding in civilian places such as hospitals [3][4].
The United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan are also pressing Israel to let more winter supplies through [2].
This strike comes as Israel’s next government is being formed: President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot on November 8 with forming a coalition, with 28 days, plus 14 more possible [9].

For you, the direct impact is small. But the situation in Gaza weighs on European diplomacy and on humanitarian aid, partly funded by European countries, and the strength of the ceasefire matters for the stability of the whole region.

United States: Trump demands $350 billion for the military before Democrats take over, but his own side doubts it has the votes

On Thursday, November 12, Donald Trump asked Senate Republican leaders to vote “IMMEDIATELY” on a $350 billion military bill, before the Democrats, winners of the midterm elections, take control of Congress in January. Several Republican senators doubt they can muster a majority [1][2][3].

On his Truth Social network, Trump wants to give American soldiers “the DECISIVE EDGE they deserve.” He accuses the incoming “radical Democrat majority” of wanting to “BLOCK and RESIST” this “historic investment” in national security [3].

The bill would go through “budget reconciliation”: a procedure that allows certain spending bills to pass by simple majority, avoiding opposition obstruction in the Senate (the “filibuster”) [3]. The project is nicknamed “Reconciliation 3.0” [6].

The Pentagon’s list: $47 billion to produce more munitions, $17 billion for the “Golden Dome,” the missile shield Trump wants, more than $48 billion for critical minerals and about $103 billion for drones, artificial intelligence and counter-drone defense [2].

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth says “$350 billion at a minimum” is needed [1]. The chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Roger Wicker, agrees: “We have to get this reconciliation passed” [3].

But Republican Senator Mike Rounds says he is not sure the bill will get 51 Republican votes, and regrets that the administration has not detailed how the money would be used [1]. Majority Leader John Thune also wonders whether he will have the 50 votes needed [1].

Senator Rick Scott supports the increase, but it must “absolutely be paid for,” and therefore offset by savings [3]. In the House, several Republicans threaten to block the bill if the administration does not get tougher on Russia [1].
The schedule is tight: few session days remain before January, and the federal government risks a partial shutdown for lack of a budget on December 11 [1].
Key takeaway: this is Trump’s last chance to pass a big military spending package without the Democrats. After January, they will control Congress and can block his spending plans [1][4].

The bill is bogged down over how to pay for it, and some lawmakers think the $350 billion figure will not be reached [1]. Senate Democratic leaders already reject any such plan before the new Congress is seated [1].

Influential Republicans warn that funding for the Golden Dome could be at risk [5]. The new Democratic majorities also plan to use the annual defense bill and the December budget deadline to cut the Pentagon’s budget, estimated at $1.5 trillion [7].
This standoff shows how much the loss of Congress now weighs on Trump [4][7].

For you, the direct impact is small. But if the United States spends far more on its own munitions and drones, it may deliver fewer, more slowly, to Europe and Ukraine. And a budget deadlock in Washington on December 11 can shake the markets, where part of Europeans’ savings is invested.

Argentina: inflation rises to 2.2% in October, more than expected, and the Milei government blames higher gas prices

On Thursday, November 12, the national statistics institute (INDEC) announced a 2.2% rise in prices in October in Argentina, versus 1.9% in September. Economists had expected less than 2%. Economy Minister Luis Caputo blames the reform of the reduced gas tariff in cold regions [1][2][3].
Over one year, prices have risen 33.1%, slightly less than September’s 33.4% [3]. Since January, they have gained 26.3% [1].
Analysts polled by Reuters expected 1.9% [3]. The central bank’s survey of economists (the “REM”) forecast 1.8%, and private consultancies 1.8% to 2.1% [1].

The housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels category rose the most: +4.2% over the month [4]. Seasonal prices, which vary with harvests, jumped 5.5%, and state-regulated prices 2.9% [4]. Some vegetables gained up to 8.8% [1].

INDEC cites three causes: tariff increases, the reduction in the volume of gas sold at subsidized prices, and the revision of the “cold zone regime,” which grants reduced tariffs to regions with harsh climates (resolution 299/2026) [4].
According to a journalist quoted by the daily Río Negro, INDEC applied this change from October 13, even though the text was only published on October 27 [4].

Luis Caputo highlights “core” inflation (excluding the most volatile prices), which fell to 1.5% from 1.7% in September, “the lowest since July 2025” in his words [2][3]. He also stresses that the year-on-year rise is slowing for the third month in a row [1].
The critical press is harsher: “Milei can’t tame inflation,” headlines the website elDiarioAR [5].

Key takeaway: falling inflation is the great success claimed by Javier Milei, but it is stalling. At 2.2% a month, prices are still rising by about a third over a year, a very high pace compared with the 2% targeted in Europe [3][1].
The rise mostly comes from government decisions: by cutting gas subsidies, the government lowers its spending, but household bills go up [4][6].

REM economists forecast 1.7% in November and 1.8% in December, so a return below 2% [1]. For opponents, the October figure shows on the contrary that the government is failing to bring inflation down durably [5].

For you, the direct effect is small. But Argentina is a major exporter of soybeans, corn and meat: its stability matters for global agricultural prices. And if you hold Argentine bonds in an “emerging markets” fund, this figure is part of what investors watch.

Pakistan: Imran Khan taken to hospital at night then returned to prison, his party demands to see him

In the night of November 10 to 11, former Prime Minister Imran Khan, who is imprisoned, was taken to a public hospital in Islamabad for an eye examination, then returned to his cell. His party, the PTI, says it learned of it from the media and demands immediate access for his family, doctors and lawyers [1][2][3].

Imran Khan was transferred from Adiala prison to the PIMS hospital in Islamabad during the night, then taken back into detention [1][2][3][5]. According to officials, doctors examined his eyes; one of them also mentioned blood pressure problems [1][4].
The hospital says he was “clinically stable” and that his general examination was “normal.” He left around 2:30 a.m. with follow-up instructions [2][3].
Khan is being treated for central retinal vein occlusion, a blockage of a vessel in the right eye, discovered after a drop in his vision. He received a series of injections in the eye [1].

The PTI demands that “his family, personal doctors and legal team” be given “immediate and unrestricted access” [1]. Its information secretary, Sheikh Waqas Akram, told Al Jazeera that Khan’s family and doctors had not been informed [1]. The party says his health must not be “a political bargaining chip” [7].

The party is demanding his transfer to the private Shifa International hospital: in August, the Supreme Court had ordered that he be treated at a private hospital in Islamabad of his choice, according to guidelines of August 18 [1][7].
The Khan family is itself targeted: two of his sisters, Uzma and Noreen, were released from a Lahore prison, but Aleema Khan remained detained nearly two months after their arrest [6].

Key takeaway: the health of Imran Khan, the country’s most popular opposition figure, has become an explosive political issue. Each discreet transfer feeds mistrust between his party and the authorities [1][7].

The climate is already tense: in October 2026, the government imposed a state of emergency in a province run by Khan’s party and suspended its local government, and the PTI had launched a march on Islamabad [6].
For months the PTI has been asking that Khan be treated outside the public system, relying on the Supreme Court decision; the authorities nonetheless took him to PIMS, a public hospital [1][2].
No media outlet reported, as of November 11, that Khan’s family or doctors had obtained the access requested [1].
For you, the direct impact is very small. But Pakistan is a nuclear power bordering India, Afghanistan and Iran: a lasting political crisis there weakens a whole region.

The yen moves back past 160 to the dollar, despite 15,400 billion yen spent this summer: Tokyo threatens to intervene again with Washington

On Thursday, November 12, the dollar crossed the 160 yen threshold for the first time since September, driven by bets on a US rate hike. On Friday, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama denounced “one-sided and rapid” moves and promised to act with the US Treasury [1][3][4].

The yen lost as much as 0.2% on Thursday and went past 160 to the dollar, a first since September [3]. It fell as low as 160.03 yen, after a “hawkish” reassessment of the path of US Federal Reserve (Fed) rates [4].
On Thursday morning, the dollar was worth 159.94 yen, its highest in more than two months [1]. On Friday, it held around 159.94 yen, with fear of an intervention limiting the yen’s decline [7].
Atsushi Mimura, the vice minister in charge of currency affairs, judged recent moves “too rapid” and said it was “too early to forget” the summer’s interventions [1][4].

On Friday, at a press conference, Satsuki Katayama said: “Recent moves in the currency market have been one-sided and rapid” [4]. She added: “We will continue to work closely with the US Treasury and respond appropriately” [2].

This summer, Tokyo spent a record 15,390 billion yen to support its currency, over three sessions between July 30 and August 3 [5]. On July 31, the United States bought 79.4 billion yen alongside it, their first intervention of this kind since 1998 [6].
The driver of the decline comes from across the Atlantic: markets now consider a Fed rate hike in December certain, and the yield on 10-year US debt has risen to 5.125% [8].

Key takeaway: the yen has almost erased the effect of the huge interventions of the summer. For Japan, each new purchase of yen costs billions of dollars of reserves, with no guarantee of success if the rate gap with the United States keeps widening [1][5][8].
The mechanism is simple: an investment in dollars pays much more than one in yen. When US rates rise further, investors sell yen to buy dollars, and the Japanese currency falls [8].
A weak yen makes the energy and food Japan imports more expensive, but boosts exporters’ profits, from carmakers to chip equipment makers, which helps the Tokyo stock market, up on Friday [9].

For you, the direct effect is limited, but tangible if you travel to Japan: your euro buys plenty there. Japanese products, from cars to cameras, also remain competitive against European brands. A sudden intervention by Tokyo can shake global markets for a few hours. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: a yen intervention

To push up its currency, Japan’s Ministry of Finance dips into its dollar reserves, built up over years, and sells them on the market in exchange for yen. This sudden demand lifts the yen, sometimes by several yen within minutes [5]. But the effect wears off if the cause remains: as long as US rates are much higher than Japanese rates, investors have an incentive to sell yen again [8]. That is why Tokyo first warns with words, as Satsuki Katayama did on Friday: the threat alone can be enough to slow sellers [2][4]. Acting with Washington, as on July 31, gives the signal more weight [6].

Cisco beats expectations and forecasts $9 billion in AI sales to cloud giants, on the evening of the Nvidia shock

On Thursday, November 12, after the close, Cisco published quarterly revenue of $18.5 billion, above the $18.1 billion expected, and raised to $9 billion its forecast for AI infrastructure sales to the big cloud operators. The stock rose after hours according to CNBC [1][2][3].
For the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year (August-October), Cisco reports $18.5 billion in revenue and net income of $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share [2].
Excluding one-time items, profit reaches $5.6 billion, or $1.40 per share, versus $1.33 expected by analysts [2][3].

The networking equipment maker raises to $9 billion its forecast for AI infrastructure sales to “hyperscalers,” the tech giants that run immense data centers [3]. CNBC headlines that this AI-related revenue will double over the fiscal year [1].
The stock market reaction remains unclear: the stock rose after the close according to CNBC, up to +4.9% according to GuruFocus, but was almost flat around $102 according to TheStreet [1][3][4].
These results come on the evening Nvidia lost 4.34% after Jensen Huang’s resignation, and the Nasdaq fell 0.39% [5].
Key takeaway: Cisco shows that the tech giants’ spending on AI continues, even when the leading chipmaker is going through a leadership crisis [1][5].

An AI data center does not run on chips alone: tens of thousands of processors have to be linked together at very high speed. That is Cisco’s business, its switches and routers, which now benefits [1][3].
For markets, these figures come after a month of doubts about AI, marked by the S&P 500’s worst session since the April 2025 tariffs, on November 5 [6].

For you, Cisco is a major stock in US indices, present in many global funds. Its results reassure about the strength of AI investment, but a forecast does not guarantee the stock will rise. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: “beating expectations”

Before each earnings release, bank analysts estimate the revenue and profit a company should report. Their average, called the “consensus,” is already built into the stock price [3]. If the company does better, like Cisco with $1.40 adjusted earnings per share versus $1.33 expected, the stock can rise [2][3]. But investors mostly look to the future: the raised forecast of $9 billion in AI sales matters more than the quarter just ended [3]. That is why a good result can sometimes leave the stock flat, if the market was hoping for even more [4].
